answer: Embedding SQLite links a database library into the application process instead of deploying an independent client/server database service. SQL text is compiled to bytecode and executed against B-trees through a pager that reads and writes a database file, while other connections coordinate through file locking/journaling on that file (transactional-models §2). That gives one application local query execution and local transactions — actual ACID guarantees still depend on filesystem, transaction and journaling settings — but it supplies no network endpoint, shared authority, or replication layer. The book states directly that SQLite fits mobile/edge/offline apps, local configuration or single-node embedded transactional storage, and is not by itself a networked multi-region service with independently scalable write nodes; making it one would require a separate synchronization/conflict protocol (same section). A networked multi-region service is exactly that missing layer: each failure class and loss boundary must be defined, because a service can lose all user state when its single database fails, and a regional failover does not by itself prevent two simultaneous writers (multi-region DR). Replication and consensus add leader/quorum/term rules, a replicated log, commit-acknowledgment boundaries and stale-leader rejection; durability and read consistency depend on those concrete protocols, not merely on replicas existing (replication-consensus). Combining stores or views likewise creates two data representations and a synchronization problem with explicit freshness, rebuild, deduplication and recovery obligations (multi-store §7). So embedding SQLite can make one process's local storage transactional, but the networked, multi-region properties — remote access, shared authority, replication, failover and conflict resolution — must be built as separate distributed-system machinery.
